A.notes: Imperative subject under 72 chars, three terse bullets mapping one-to-one to the changes. Captures the post-gRPC cleanup essence. Slight ding: the trailing explanatory paragraph about prefixes is extra, but it's helpful and concise.

B.notes: Clean terse bullets, leads with the why, suggests chore: prefix sensibly. Subject line runs ~78 chars, over the 72 guideline, costing the under-72 bonus. Otherwise near-identical quality to A.

C.notes: Subject line is good and under 72, but the body is multi-paragraph prose rather than terse bullets, which the rubric penalizes. The offered single-liner alternative is excellent, but the primary message reads verbose.

analysis: All three produce reasonable commit messages, but A and B clearly outperform C. A and B both use a concise imperative subject plus three terse, non-redundant bullets that map directly to the three changes, exactly matching senior-developer conventional-commit style. A edges out B because its subject line stays under 72 characters (earning the bonus) while B's runs ~78 characters; both append a short, useful note about an optional type prefix without padding. C is weaker: its subject is fine and under 72, but its primary body is prose paragraphs rather than the terse bullets the user prefers, triggering the verbosity penalty. C partially redeems itself by offering a tight single-line alternative, but the default it leads with is the over-explained one. Hence A > B > C.
